questions.text: Under Group 9, why is the architect's fee set at 150% of the basic fee rather than 100% when the project involves renovation of an existing building?

options.text: Because renovation projects require a higher profit margin for the architect, reflecting increased financial risk
Because the PRBoA imposes a surcharge on all renovation permits, increasing overall project costs
Because renovation work demands more architectural effort due to existing conditions, structural constraints, and as-built documentation requirements
Because the contractor's fee is also increased by 150% for renovation work, aligning with industry standards

rationale.a: The multiplier addresses increased design effort, not profit margin. The architect's overhead and profit structure remains the same.
rationale.b: The 150% multiplier is a fee guideline in the Architect's Guidelines, not a surcharge imposed by the PRBoA on building permits.
rationale.d: Group 9 addresses the architect's fee only. The contractor's compensation is determined separately through the construction contract.
rationale.correct: Renovation projects inherently require more design effort than new construction of equivalent scope. The architect must assess existing conditions, work within structural constraints, produce or verify as-built documentation, and design solutions that integrate with existing building systems. The 150% multiplier compensates for this additional effort.
rationale.takeaway: Renovation = 150% because working with existing conditions demands more effort than new construction — the multiplier compensates for this, not for higher profit.

questions.text: Under the Architect's Guidelines, what is the recommended fee percentage for a Group 1 project (Simplest Utilization and Character) with a Project Construction Cost of ₱50 million or less?

options.text: 5% DAEDS of PCC
6% DAEDS of PCC
7% DAEDS of PCC
8% DAEDS of PCC

rationale.b: 6% is the base rate for Group 2 (Moderate Complexity), not Group 1.
rationale.c: 7% is the base rate for Group 3 (Exceptional Character), not Group 1.
rationale.d: 8% is an outdated rate from the 1979 UAP schedule — the Architect's Guidelines revised these percentages.
rationale.correct: the Architect's Guidelines specifies that Group 1 (Simplest Utilization and Character) projects with PCC of ₱50M or less carry a DAEDS fee of 5% of PCC.
rationale.takeaway: Group 1 = 5% DAEDS, Group 2 = 6% DAEDS, Group 3 = 7% DAEDS — the complexity groups ascend by 1% each according to the Architect's Guidelines.

questions.text: What is the key difference between Group 6 (Repetitive Building) and Group 7 (Repetitive Housing) in how fees are structured?

options.text: Group 6 uses a flat percentage while Group 7 uses the MDPE method, which involves detailed cost analysis and adjustments
Group 6 applies declining percentages of the basic fee per repeated building, while Group 7 starts at 10% of PCC and adds incremental amounts per additional unit
Group 6 applies to residential projects and Group 7 applies to commercial projects, with different fee structures based on project type
Group 6 charges 150% of the basic fee while Group 7 charges 100% of the basic fee, reflecting the complexity and scale of the projects

rationale.a: Neither group uses the MDPE method — both use variations of the percentage-of-PCC approach. MDPE is reserved for Group 10.
rationale.c: The reverse is closer: Group 6 applies to repeated non-residential buildings (schools, branch offices), while Group 7 applies to mass housing developments.
rationale.d: The 150% multiplier belongs to Group 9 (Renovations), not Group 6. Group 6 starts at 100% for the first building and declines from there.
rationale.correct: Group 6 uses a declining schedule based on percentages of the basic fee (1st at 100%, 2nd at 80%, 3rd at 60%, rest at 40%). Group 7 starts at 10% of PCC for the 1st unit and adds increments (+60% for 2nd–10th, then +30% for 11th onward).
rationale.takeaway: Group 6 = declining from 100% of basic fee per building; Group 7 = 10% base plus incremental additions per housing unit.

questions.text: An architect is commissioned to design a Group 1 warehouse with a PCC of ₱120 million. Using the sliding sclea, what is the architect's total fee?

rationale.b: ₱6,300,000 results from using the outdated 6% base rate instead of the correct the Architect's Guidelines rate of 5%.
rationale.c: ₱7,200,000 applies a flat 6% to the entire ₱120M — this ignores the sliding scale and uses the wrong base rate.
rationale.d: ₱6,000,000 results from applying only two brackets (₱50M + ₱50M) instead of three, leaving the final ₱20M uncounted.
rationale.takeaway: Group 1 uses the 5% DAEDS base (per the Architect's Guidelines), then slides to 4%, 3%, 2%, 1%, 0.5% on successive brackets.

questions.text: Which Project Classification Group covers low-rise residential buildings such as single-family houses, duplexes, and townhouses?

options.text: Group 1 — Simplest Utilization and Character
Group 3 — Exceptional Character
Group 4 — Low-Rise Residentials
Group 7 — Repetitive Housing

rationale.a: Group 1 covers buildings of simplest utilization and character — utilitarian structures like warehouses and simple factories, not residentials.
rationale.b: Group 3 covers buildings of exceptional character housing special equipment — churches, theaters, museums — not standard residential buildings.
rationale.d: Group 7 covers repetitive housing (mass housing developments with a single unit design repeated), not the general low-rise residential category.
rationale.correct: Group 4 covers residences such as single-detached, duplexes, rowhouses, small apartment houses, and townhouses.
rationale.takeaway: Low-rise residentials = Group 4 at 10% of PCC — distinct from repetitive housing (Group 7) and utilitarian structures (Group 1).

questions.explanation: Group 1 covers buildings of simplest utilization and character — utilitarian structures like warehouses and simple factories, not residentials. Group 3 covers buildings of exceptional character housing special equipment — churches, theaters, museums — not standard residential buildings. Group 7 covers repetitive housing (mass housing developments with a single unit design repeated), not the general low-rise residential category. Group 4 covers residences such as single-detached, duplexes, rowhouses, small apartment houses, and townhouses. Low-rise residentials = Group 4 at 10% of PCC — distinct from repetitive housing (Group 7) and utilitarian structures (Group 1).

questions.text: A developer commissions an architect to design a subdivision with 15 identical housing units under Group 7 (Repetitive Housing). What fee structure applies to the 12th unit?

options.text: 60% of the basic fee for each additional unit, calculated based on the total construction cost of the unit
40% of the basic fee for each additional unit, provided the design remains unchanged from the original
The fee of the 10th unit plus 30% for each additional unit
10% of PCC as a flat rate for every unit after the 10th, regardless of any modifications made to the design

rationale.a: The +60% increment applies to the 2nd through 10th units, not units beyond the 10th.
rationale.b: 40% of basic fee is the Group 6 (Repetitive Building) rate for the 4th building onward — this is a different group with a different calculation basis.
rationale.d: The fee is not a flat 10% for every unit beyond the 10th. The 10% of PCC applies to the 1st unit only; subsequent units use the incremental formula.
rationale.correct: Under Group 7, units from the 11th onward are charged at the fee of the 10th unit plus 30% for each additional unit. The 12th unit falls in this bracket.
rationale.takeaway: Group 7 has three tiers: 1st unit at 10%, 2nd–10th at +60% each, 11th onward at fee of 10th + 30% each.

questions.text: An architect classifies a laboratory building with specialized equipment as Group 3 (Exceptional Character) with a PCC of ₱250 million. The client argues it should be Group 2 (Moderate Complexity) because the building uses standard construction methods. Under the Architect's Guidelines, which classification is correct, and what is the fee difference between the two interpretations?

options.text: Group 2 is correct because standard construction methods determine the group; fee difference is ₱1,000,000
Group 3 is correct because it covers buildings housing special equipment; fee difference is ₱2,500,000
Group 3 is correct because it covers buildings housing special equipment; fee difference is ₱500,000
Group 3 is correct because it covers buildings housing special equipment; fee difference is ₱1,500,000

rationale.a: Group 2 is incorrect. The Architect's Guidelines classify by building function and character, not solely by construction method. Special equipment is a Group 3 criterion.
rationale.c: Group 3 is correct, but ₱500,000 understates the difference. The ₱250M project spans four rate brackets, not just one. Each bracket differs by 1% between groups.
rationale.d: Group 3 is correct, but ₱1,500,000 still understates the difference. A ₱250M project spans four brackets (₱50M each at different rates), not just 1.5 brackets.
rationale.correct: Group 3 explicitly covers buildings of exceptional character AND those housing special equipment. A laboratory building qualifies under Group 3 regardless of its structural system. Per the Architect's Guidelines sliding scale: Group 3 = (7%, 6%, 5%, 4%, 3%, 2%), Group 2 = (6%, 5%, 4%, 3%, 2%, 1%). For ₱250M: Group 3 = (₱50M × 7%) + (₱50M × 6%) + (₱100M × 5%) + (₱50M × 4%) = ₱3,500,000 + ₱3,000,000 + ₱5,000,000 + ₱2,000,000 = ₱13,500,000. Group 2 = (₱50M × 6%) + (₱50M × 5%) + (₱100M × 4%) + (₱50M × 3%) = ₱3,000,000 + ₱2,500,000 + ₱4,000,000 + ₱1,500,000 = ₱11,000,000. Difference = ₱2,500,000. Each bracket differs by 1%, and ₱250M spans four brackets (₱50M + ₱50M + ₱100M + ₱50M), so total difference = 1% on each bracket.
rationale.takeaway: For large projects spanning multiple rate brackets, the cumulative fee difference between adjacent complexity groups grows substantially. Group 3's 1% premium over Group 2 on each bracket compounds across the entire ₱250M PCC.

questions.text: An architect is engaged to renovate an existing Group 3 building (Exceptional Character) with a PCC of ₱30 million. What is the architect's fee under Group 9?

rationale.a: ₱2,100,000 is the base fee for Group 3 new construction (₱30M × 7%), but this answer omits the 150% renovation multiplier under Group 9.
rationale.c: ₱3,000,000 results from incorrectly applying 10% of PCC (Group 4 rate) instead of the correct Group 3 DAEDS rate of 7%.
rationale.d: ₱4,500,000 results from applying 150% to an incorrect base — likely using an outdated 8% rate instead of the correct the Architect's Guidelines rate of 7%.
rationale.correct: Step 1: Determine base fee as if new construction under Group 3. Since ₱30M is ≤ ₱50M, apply flat 7% DAEDS rate = ₱30M × 7% = ₱2,100,000. Step 2: Apply Group 9 renovation multiplier = ₱2,100,000 × 150% = ₱3,150,000.
rationale.takeaway: Group 9 renovation fee = base group fee × 150%. Group 3 base is 7% DAEDS per the Architect's Guidelines.

questions.text: Why do the Architect's Guidelines apply a sliding sclea to Group 1–3 projects with PCC exceeding ₱50 million, rather than a flat percentage on the entire PCC?

options.text: Because the architect's liability decreases as the project cost increases, reflecting a reduced risk profile for larger projects.
Because architectural effort does not increase proportionally with construction cost beyond a certain project size
Because the PRBoA mandates fee reductions for projects over ₱50 million, ensuring affordability for large-scale developments.
Because larger projects always use the MDPE compensation method instead, which aligns fees with project complexity rather than cost.

rationale.a: Liability does not decrease with project size — in fact, larger projects may carry greater liability exposure. The sliding scale addresses fee proportionality, not liability.
rationale.c: The sliding scale is established in the Architect's Guidelines as a professional standard, not mandated by the PRBoA as a regulatory fee reduction.
rationale.d: Larger projects under Groups 1–3 still use the percentage-of-PCC method with the sliding scale — MDPE is specified for Group 10 (Technical Expertise), not as an alternative for large projects.
rationale.correct: The sliding scale reflects the economic reality that design effort increases at a diminishing rate as project cost rises. A ₱1 billion warehouse does not require 20 times the design effort of a ₱50M warehouse, so the fee rate decreases on the excess amount.
rationale.takeaway: The sliding scale exists because design effort does not scale linearly with construction cost — the percentage decreases as PCC increases.

questions.text: A client presents two projects to an architect: Project A is a new Group 2 office building with ₱80M PCC, and Project B is the renovation of an existing Group 1 warehouse with ₱45M PCC. Which project yields the higher architect's fee, and by how much?

options.text: Project A at ₱4,500,000 vs. Project B at ₱3,375,000 — Project A is higher by ₱1,125,000
Project A at ₱5,600,000 vs. Project B at ₱2,700,000 — Project A is higher by ₱2,900,000
Project A at ₱5,000,000 vs. Project B at ₱2,700,000 — Project A is higher by ₱2,300,000
Project B at ₱4,050,000 vs. Project A at ₱3,500,000 — Project B is higher by ₱550,000

rationale.b: ₱5,600,000 for Project A results from applying an outdated 7% base rate. ₱2,700,000 for Project B applies the wrong Group 1 base rate (6% instead of 5%) and is missing the renovation multiplier.
rationale.c: Project A uses wrong base rate (7% instead of 6%). Project B at ₱2,700,000 uses wrong base rate (6% instead of 5%) and omits the Group 9 renovation multiplier of 150%.
rationale.d: This reverses which project is higher and uses outdated percentage rates from the 1979 UAP schedule.
rationale.correct: Project A (Group 2, ₱80M): First ₱50M × 6% DAEDS = ₱3,000,000; next ₱30M (₱50M–₱100M bracket) × 5% = ₱1,500,000; total = ₱4,500,000. Project B (Group 1 renovation under Group 9, ₱45M): Base fee = ₱45M × 5% DAEDS = ₱2,250,000; renovation multiplier = ₱2,250,000 × 150% = ₱3,375,000. Project A is higher by ₱1,125,000.
rationale.takeaway: Per the Architect's Guidelines: Group 1 = 5%, Group 2 = 6%. Apply sliding scale for projects over ₱50M, and multiply by 150% for Group 9 renovations.
